transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Radai.
I'm your host, Edipalmian, and today we're excited to have Andrew Hollingworth on the show.
Andrew is an experienced investor based in the UK, where he is the founder and portfolio manager of Holland Advisors.
For this episode, he has selected the book 1929, written by Andrew Ross Sorkin.
We think the book is a fantastic read, as it's vividly describing the most significant financial disaster in modern history.
And we highly recommend investors and non-investors to read it.
1929 was published in October 2025, and we're thrilled to discuss it on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Andrew Hollingworth.
Hello Andrew and welcome to Investing by the Books Podcast.
Thank you so much for having me.
Where are we reaching you?
I'm in France, currently, actually. I'm having a bit of time to sort of doing a little bit of skiing and a little bit of time to do a bit of thinking, actually.
So I'm mostly based in the UK, but now, again, it's quite nice to get away.
Great. And to begin, can you tell our listeners about your path to becoming a professional investor?
A path to a professional investor.
I was non-traditional, I suppose, as the way you did in the sense that I didn't go to college.
I joined the industry when I was 18 years old.
I did sort of various clerical sort of back-office jobs.
Took my analyst exams and then just gradually worked my way through various sort of junior jobs to become a stock broker, to become a farm manager.
But yeah, I just sort of self-taught along the way, worked with some good people, got a few lucky breaks.
But I started before the crash in 1987, so that may or may not become relevant to the discussion we're about to have next.
And what are you doing today, otherwise?
I was just doing some reading and just sort of researching a few companies. So yeah, just sort of normal day.
Wonderful. And for this episode, we will speak about the book 1929. Can you briefly tell us what is it about?
1929 is obviously about the crack of 1929.
And I certainly have, and maybe some of your listeners will have researched this sort of period of time before and let other books on the subject.
This is quite an interesting book because it's not about the economics. It's not about, you know, the stock market, per se, and the working for the stock market.
It's about the people and about the different players in the sort of game, if you would call it that, the politicians, the bankers, all the various sort of regulators.
And it tells their story of sort of who prist and overconfidence and all the rest of it.
So, you know, it's a really interesting account because it feels like you're reading it real-time, not a hundred years later.
And for those who haven't read it, how is it structured?
It is structured by a succession of stories and following different people's lives.
So there may be, so for example, Winston Churchill, you wouldn't expect it necessarily, but Winston Churchill's in the book.
And Winston Churchill features sort of four or five times throughout the book, telling his sort of real life experiences of what happened to him during that period of time.
And obviously, Roosevelt's in the book, you'd expect.
And there are lots and lots of other bankers and brokers, but you're told what they did in 1927 and 1929 in 1931.
So you're following their life story through the period, as I say, not reflecting on what it would like, sort of, you know, six, seven years later from an academic perspective.
The author of the book is Andrew Ross Sorkin. Who is he?
So he's one of the sort of main anchors on TNBC. So if you turn on your investing television, you know, and you're watching the USC and BC, he's one of the main anchors.
He's on CNBC pretty much every day.
And so I wouldn't necessarily have him down as sort of a great authority on sort of these sorts of chapters in history because he's a commentator on today.
He's not a study of history.
But he also wrote the book, Too Big to Fail, which was a really excellent book and made into an, I'm sure you've seen it in the next film.
And I think that sort of gave him the sort of the breadth if you like to go back and study this period of time.
And he's, you know, this is not a, this is not a commentary by, you know, a TV commentator.
This is a detailed long, long, long study of many, many people's participants in this period of time.
So it's to say he's an anchor, it doesn't perhaps do the book any justice.
But there are multiple books of the crash and the following depression, of course.
Why do you think this one is worth reading?
I think this is about the site.
I'm another big fan of the market cycles.
I'm a big fan of how marks and the big fan of the sort of psychology of investing and how it isn't really about numbers.
And it's about stories and it's about people and it's about, you know, the madness of crowds and the crazy things that we collectively do when we think we're all being logically, if you like.
And so I mean, you're reading books about Tuneit mainly and all the rest of it.
And I think this is exactly what this is.
But it's not necessarily, as I say, about the economics.
It's about watching, indeed, be quite bright or no very bright, very well connected, very wealthy, influential people.
Basically do a succession of incredibly dumb things.
And that's sort of fascinating from a sort of internal reflection perspective, maybe.
And were there any surprises for you when you read the book?
The amount of greed in the run up to this period of time was absolutely enormous.
And it was everywhere in society.
And everybody wanted a part of it.
It was, you know, the influential celebrities of the day, whether it be sportsman, whether it be politicians, whether it be general public.
Everybody wanted to play the game and to be part of the greed game, if you like.
And the population would just like addicted to get rich, quick schemes.
And sadly, as we saw in 2008, you know, first-hand ourselves Wall Street was happy to sell these schemes in as big of quantities as anybody wanted to buy them.
And so it's sort of gained, just spiraled on and spiraled on.
So there are real echoes in 2008 of this period of time.
But then there are obviously some differences as well.
And I think the one thing I would say I'd really call out is I think how just self-serving everybody was.
I mean, it's amazing.
You think, oh, well, there's these regulators and these politicians and they're all going to try and do the right thing.
And it's only the bankers that agree to you.
And actually, that isn't how it came across at all.
A lot of the politicians were pretty self-serving as well and not very few people were trying to do what was right for the greater good.
And why do you think this happened in the 1920s and in the US?
I don't really know actually.
I think like all these sort of cycles, they sort of have a life of their own and they sort of build up.
But I haven't really studied the period sort of in the 1910s or whatever else.
There's obviously the First World War and all the stuff that came from that and you could reach from that.
I haven't really studied all that.
And I think, you know, what is relevant or more sort of appropriate, I think is the fact that we didn't really have the Federal Reserve in a proper structure like in this today.
We didn't have the sort of deposit insurance scheme like it is in the structure today.
And so I think if those institutions were in place, then I think this would have been a sort of 2008 type event.
But because those institutions weren't in place, this became like a sort of epoch event that sort of changed the whole banking sector.
And so I think that that, I think what became before was just probably another ridiculous boom like we saw in 2005 to 2008.
But it was how it was handled that made it such a sort of defining period.
Good point. And I think when you read the run-up to the 1929 that is also described in the book, it's clear that credit played a fundamental role in this.
And people started buying cars and they borrowed a lot of money for that. And one quote that was in the book is that stocks were no different than a vacuum cleaner or a dishwasher.
They were all products that improved your life. I think that was quite telling.
I think that's right. And I think the, there's always products to improve all of our lives.
But I think maybe this was the first period of time that credit was widely available and the flip side of credit in the sense that it can ruin you just perhaps wasn't really understood.
And so credit was, I mean the bit that struck me in the book is that you get unsophisticated people that borrowed a bit of money to invest on margin.
Well, that's always happening today. And there's always unfortunate people who don't really understand the rules of the game and they get themselves into terrible trouble because of that.
What's really noticeable at this book is that you know, you had sort of really seen the bankers, people are already being paid millions and pounds, millions of dollars a year, whatever else. Who were then investing on margin?
Well, why on earth would you, if you're already one of the wealthiest people in America, would you invest on margin?
But everybody did and lots and lots of people who were already very rich, which is phenomenally greedy and then got ruined because of the greed.
And that's a bit that really struck me as being unusual because that's, that's a bit like, you know, Jamie Dimon borrowing five times his salary to go and invest in other stocks in the stock market.
You just don't see that in most periods of time that we've covered.
And were there any stories or examples of this greed that stood out for you that you remember from the book?
I can't remember the individual name because it was about a month ago that I read the book.
But yeah, I mean, there are, there was one particular banker who was profiled in the book and he's sort of like the head of six group at the time type individual.
And ultimately he seems to be sort of the face of Wall Street and and people hadn't really realized that, you know, while he was being sort of the person that was encouraging the general public and everyone to invest in Wall Street and was doing the right things.
Behind the scenes, he was financed to a falling apart and was borrowing money from JP Morgan and other people to hold his whole his life together if you like.
So it was just, it was a sort of poster child of populist investing, but ultimately was falling apart financially behind the scenes.
And that only came out sort of in 1934, 1935 when he's leveraging and the fact that he had to go to JP Morgan to get financing himself became apparent.
So yeah, that's sort of, it's a sort of gradual unpeeling of an onion to realize that the center of it was actually rocked.
Yeah, Charles Mitchell was his name or he was called that you are quite right. Thank you.
You've read it more recently than me. I read it back in October type or November type.
Charles Mitchell, you're quite right.
Yeah, and Sunshine Charlie was his nickname because he was such an optimist, but he managed to bring a national city bank to one of the biggest or it was about to be the largest bank in the world actually.
At the peak of everything.
You're right. And he is one of the characters throughout the book.
And you see his sort of how incredibly important he was and influential he was to both the popular population and to Walter politician.
And then gradually how does I say that onion gets unpeeled and he falls apart and it's remarkable really.
Yeah, and I don't want to spoil all of the golden nuggets for you listeners who haven't read the book yet.
But one example of this exuberance that existed was the astrologist Evangelin Adams.
Do you remember her from the book?
I'm afraid I don't. You're going to have to recount me.
As I said, I love my wife with Joe Ketchy because I love the messages that I get from books and stories that I get from books.
But you obviously have a better recall than I do.
I mean, I read it as I say about six weeks or six or eight weeks ago now.
So please recount that if you want to.
The funny thing is that you have an astrologist who becomes so influential on Wall Street and she gives stock pick advice based on your sodium sign.
So as an investor you can go to her and get to know which stock should I buy.
And she had 100,000 subscribers to her newsletter and this was in 1929 in September.
She moved to her office to Carnegie Hall and she said that the Dow Jones could climb to heaven.
But clearly she had a good understanding of human nature and could extract some value from that.
Exactly right. Exactly right.
So many stories were quite right. It's very interesting.
But are there any other highlights from the book that you would like to mention some lessons?
Yeah, I mean, there's some other things I would say.
I think I mentioned it a little wrong.
I think in the sense that the fact that the institutions that we have today didn't exist or didn't exist in the current forms.
We didn't have deposit protection insurance was really, really crucial.
And I think that's something that I think we should be very grateful to the participants.
Sort of on the top bailouts in 2008 and what they did with the institutions that were available.
So that was a real noticeable difference for me.
And the other highlights I would say is that I thought the Roosevelt Hoover situation was fascinating in the sense that Roosevelt's gone down in history.
It's been this great president.
And Hoover is being sort of, you know, a bit sort of Tom pesky and if you like.
And actually I didn't read it that way at all.
I read that Hoover was trying very hard during the and over to Roosevelt to try to get to Roosevelt to step in and to sort of address the banking crisis.
And Roosevelt was having none of it.
He was basically like, well, is your problem? I don't care.
And I'm going to sort of sort of sort of out when I get inaugurated in eight weeks time.
And in that eight week period, no, the banking sets are literally collapsed.
And I think, you know, it's really interesting.
And if you look at the context of history, how these people are perceived.
And the other thing is I haven't got the question from to me.
And maybe you have and I did put it in my right up of it is I remember there was a quote by Churchill in the Churchill in the book.
And literally it was like the week after or three weeks after the stock market crash, whatever it was.
And he basically had a quote along the lines of just how despite the fact that there were people, you know, the person that threw themselves out of the hotel window above him.
And how he was talking about how society was sort of falling apart, you know, behind in front of his very eyes.
He said, but anybody, any, you know, European or UK skeptic of the, you know, American financial model needs to realize that they'll rise again.
And the, you know, the American sort of dream is not dead and the capitalism will will endure.
That's not that's not the quote, but that's the essence of what he said.
And that to be was absolutely amazing.
And pressing it and bearing in mind, this is like on the eve of the end of capitalism as some people would see it.
And yet ultimately what he said was absolutely correct in the context of the history we can now see.
Yeah. And on that theme, I think it's, it's a good lesson as well, that there is always hope and hope refused to die.
I mean, we saw so many examples of the following during the following years because this book is, it's called 1929, but it covers a few more years after that as well.
And there were a number of rallies in the stock market and a lot of optimism, at least, at least in the markets.
Yeah, I think that's true. I think that's true.
But I mean, I suppose the other thing that I really, really realized that I think we saw this again after 2008.
And I think it's very interesting today, actually.
So we're not going to get involved today's politics, but I think it's interesting that we've wasted a very long time before we've eased the banking regulation in the world now.
And we're like 20 years after 2008, before we've done so.
And the study of 1929 is the same.
It's a lot of the regulations, Glass-Steagall and all the rest of it and all the unwinding of Charles Mitchell's, you know,
the court cases that followed on from that didn't take six months or a year.
They took five or six years to take place.
So the knock on unwind, the knock on investigation, the knock on new regulations were five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten years in coming.
And I think that's why these periods of time have such long effects.
It's because the knee jet reaction of what went wrong is still being done in 1935.
I've all went wrong in 1928, basically.
At the core of it, it's about trust, I think, because that's, if you don't have trust, then the system doesn't work.
What's your view on that?
Of course. And I think, but at the end of the day, most of the participants in this, you know, most investors don't think that hard about it.
They just want to make money.
And if they make money tomorrow, they've got confidence for the day after and so on.
But if they lose a lot of money and they permanently lose a lot of money and they feel they've been deceived,
then their trust in the system evaporates. And the suspicion and the finger pointing, you know, becomes worse and worse and worse.
And I think that's, you know, the politicians and the regulatory knock on effects, five, ten years down the line,
are mostly because the, you know, the, the electric, the, the, the electorate is asking them pushing them to do that, because it wants,
to prevent your payback for what it sees as a misdemeanors of the past.
And we saw a lot of that post the back in crisis and I don't think it was any different, you know, post 1929.
Anything else that you would like to mention from the book?
I don't think so. I think that's mostly it. I think the self-serving nature of people and the fact that greed was everywhere and leverage was everywhere came through.
But yeah, it's just a great story of the psychology of markets, I think.
And is there something that you think could have made the book even better?
Hard to think that when you think you spread a real cracker.
I don't think so, actually. I mean, it was a little long, maybe, but I think, you know, that's, I actually listened to it as an audio book. I didn't read it.
So I had like two long plane journeys and I listened to it literally the length. But I, but I couldn't turn it off.
It was absolutely addictive in terms of these characters and I was living these characters alive.
So no, I thought of, I couldn't fault it.
Great. And if we go over to your professional life, you are the founder of Holland Advisors that you set up in 2008.
Can you tell us a bit about the firm?
Yeah, I mean, 2008, I set up the business on my own. We very much were trying to produce investment research for professional investors along the lines of what Buffett and Munger would approach.
And that was my job for quite a long period of time as an independent researcher. And then in 2011, we set up our own fund.
And, you know, and that's the fund that we run today. Just from one fund. It's a global fund. It's a long, only fund.
It, for Europeans, it's a usage structure, but, you know, it's some sort of US mutual fund, you know, style in the way that it works.
Yeah, and it's my hobby and it's my job and I love it.
And how do you differentiate from, from other investors?
As the years have gone on, I mean, I started an industry in 1987 and I didn't, I wasn't given a guidebook about how to do the job.
I just gone on this sort of self-educated course and that's vastly been about Munger sleep, Ben Gray and Templeton, and studying all these various people.
And I think this time goes on, you just learn certain things. And I realize now that I, certain traits I believe you have to follow to get great compounding.
And I didn't really realize until we went marketing our fund two or three years ago to the wider population.
How different those perhaps those traits are from a standard, you know, fund run by European money manager API.
So yeah, I'm very, very passionate about global, very passionate about going anywhere, about an open mind, but particularly about businesses having powerful sustainable competitive advantages and having brilliant owner managers.
And if those two things aren't pretty obvious, pretty quickly, I'm just not that interested because there's just so many other people looking at so many other bits of undervaluational, systematic approaches.
And that's not my game. My game is I want to find brilliant businesses that are run by exceptional owner managers and invest at times when everyone else thinks I'm wrong.
And how do you go about figuring out if they are brilliant, the businesses and the people?
I think working out where the businesses are brilliant or not does take a lot of preparation.
So, you know, my up into Omaha, I don't know, seven or eight times now, you know, listen to Buffett talk about notes and I've done what everyone else has done and I've looked at branded businesses and all the rest of it.
And I think the reality of that is is that these days is pretty table stakes is pretty sort of everyone's doing that.
I think you need to really understand what makes businesses powerful and if you're readers of or listeners have never watched it already, I would read them seven pounds by Hamilton Helmer.
And it's a book that basically talks about sustainable competitive advantages and talks about things like network effects and scale economy shared and all the rest of it.
And those are then our business models that are equally powerful to say notes, but the stock market hasn't fully understood them.
And then you're into the interesting realm to view, you can see a business model that's powerful that maybe the rest of the stock market can't see as powerful.
And therefore you're getting value at the point of investment.
And that is, you know, you can't just have one lever that says I want a motor and it's a brand because that's just the one lever that you need lots and lots and lots of different levers to go right.
Well, I'm going to pull that one today and that one tomorrow.
And so I think it takes a long time to get that whole spectrum.
It's a bit like playing bridge or cards. You need to have seven or eight or 10 ways to play a hand.
And that I think is what takes a long time to develop.
Is that influencing how concentrated you are in the portfolio?
A little bit in the sense that I mean, we own about 30 stocks, 25 to 30 or so, which is about as few as we can only know structure.
So we have to have a certain amount of diversification to run the long way of the structure we've got.
But in all truths, if you ask me to add a portfolio of 50 stocks, I think I'd struggle to find them.
And I'm looking globally and I'm looking across all sectors.
So yeah, I've got a pretty open remit to be able to buy anything within reason.
But I can only find 25 or 30 or 35 at any one point in time.
So either I'm just not working very hard, which I think I am.
Or I'm being very, very selective, which is I think is what we are doing.
And that's pretty consistent with how the other great investors in the past have done this job.
They haven't own 50 or 100 stocks. They own five or 10 or 20.
And they've searched high and low and been very selective in choosing those.
You mentioned that you want to buy these companies at a great valuation.
How long do you typically want to hold them?
In a perfect world forever.
I mean, I'm in the Charlie Munger camp that, you know, the investment return you're going to earn from the business.
The long view on it is going to be closer to the return on capital.
It actually makes as a business in terms of the market or capital it can deploy.
So I mean, we've got a couple of investments in the fund, which are wise and new holdings.
And those businesses, you know, I've got long, long ways of growth and make high returns on capital on the money they deploy today.
Now, if that's the case and if you can find a business like businesses like that,
well, yeah, you want to make sure you're not outrageously ever paying from the time that you purchased them.
But otherwise, you're one way to put a brain on time.
Now, there are other companies in the fund that were perhaps so when we bought Meta,
we had about five percent of the fund invested in Meta at about $150.
Now, you know, an assessment of Meta at $150 is quite different to an assessment of it at $600.
I still own it in the fund.
But you know, you are slightly more opportunistic in terms of the recovery that other business like that has taken place
and maybe how long you might own that side of that position for.
So it does slightly different differ on the quality of the business and the longevity and its growth
and how much of the upside that you saw when you bought the business was in its long-term compounding
and how much of it was in its cheap.
And what's your view on trimming holdings?
On trimming them.
Ultimately, all I'm doing is just trying to, you know, metaphorically,
I've got a hundred pounds worth of capital to deploy all the time.
And so I don't have to target prices.
I don't make myself sell something just because it's gone up.
But I have to redeploy capital.
If I find a new idea, I've got to find the capital from the existing portfolio effectively to invest in that new idea.
And so effectively, a good idea earns its own paid place in the portfolio.
And that's the main reason why we're trimming, if you like.
I mean, obviously selling is perhaps a different decision.
And that's a, it's just gone up so much that you just can't see the upside anymore.
Or you've made a mistake.
But from a trimming perspective, I don't really do it.
I want to run our best positions.
And I want to be sort of in that by right sit tight campaigner sort of company.
You mentioned in the beginning that you started in 1987.
And you obviously experienced a number of crisis since then.
And now we're talking about a 1929 book as well.
So I have to ask you how you're dealing with this type of market distress situations.
I really enjoy actually now.
I think the first couple of cycles you go through are slightly terrifying.
And you either lose your job or you lose your money.
Or you make terrible mistakes because I don't know you've borrowed money or whatever you do.
And then maybe the second cycle you go through isn't financially paid me quite so awful for you.
But maybe you've realised all the clever spreadsheets you've built for forecasting companies, forecasts and nonsense.
So you learn a bit of who breaks from that.
And then the third cycle you go through, I think you might start to make some money because you actually start to know that these things come along.
And so you've got capital to deploy or you sell a business that's gone down 20% and you put it in the business that's gone down 80%.
And I think as you get older and you see more of these cycles, you can see them for what they are.
And you realise that they come along in the course of time.
And so now I don't look forward to them.
But you know as Buffett I think famously said, you know, it's not like we like fair markets per se.
But we like the prices they bring.
And that's how I feel about it now.
And I think there's a big difference between the sort of political cycle and an economic cycle and the market cycle.
And everyone talks about the political cycle and the economic cycle is all time.
But the market cycle can be completely different.
And that's the one that really investors we need to understand a bit better and just be aware that they take place and we need to manage our way through them.
So I don't upset me anymore now.
I'm just sort of used to them now.
Interesting.
And are you actively managing a cash position based on this?
No, not really.
Not really.
In the fund, I'm pretty much fully invested.
We run maybe a two to five or six percent cash position most of the time.
What's interesting actually is the market downturns.
I tend to have a good look at portfolio as you'd expect from a risk perspective.
But because I've got a lot of owner managers and entrepreneurs in 90 percent of my fund that you invested in entrepreneurial businesses,
most of those businesses don't come with leverage.
Most of them come with cash on the balance sheet.
So actually by investing alongside entrepreneurs who take a very long term, you've often got a much better balance sheet you might have in non entrepreneurial companies.
So I'm not actually managing cycle, but often those entrepreneurs are helping me have dry powder when they come along, let's say.
So yeah, they're all different ways to navigate them.
And I don't necessarily think trying to call them is a good idea.
Just accepting that they take place is more helping.
So the risk would rather be that some of your investors would pull out some money at the worst of times?
Yeah, I'm delighted to say that that hasn't happened so far in the sense that the downturns we have had seem almost no redemptions whatsoever in the funds.
And I think everyone has their own decisions to make.
And I think as an investor manager, your job is to communicate as openly and as candidly and honestly as you can.
And if you do that, then hopefully people realize what you're trying to do and that they don't redeem from your fund.
Equally, I think at the point that which people invest in your fund, you need to be candid about what you can and can't do.
So we had a brilliant year sort of 2023, 2024, but we had a pretty poor year, 2022, because I own consumer stocks, I didn't own defense, I didn't own oil, I didn't own utilities.
So I owned all the things that went down and none of the things that went up, but that's just an output of looking at entrepreneurial led businesses.
They're not in those utility types sectors, but I'm very open with people about that.
And I think they know that that's what they're getting.
And I think that's part of the game, I think, is to be very clear and not to pretend that you can, you know, somehow avoid cycles, both for yourself or for the investors who's capable of looking after.
Sounds like you have earned the investors trust.
Well, I don't know.
If we look ahead five or ten years, what are your ambitions and is there anything that you would like to have learned by them?
Gosh, I don't know really, I mean, I'm really lucky in terms of where I am now already in the sense that, you know, what do you really want, you want to be able to run capital the way that you think it should be run, not in a mandate that's dictated to you.
And you want to be open to be able to keep learning all the whole time.
And that's sort of where I am.
And okay, there's some, there's difficulties about running your own business and there's complexities and there's regulation and all that stuff that, you know, it makes life less pleasant.
But for the vast majority of the time, I'm able to do the job in exactly the way I want to do it.
And that's great. That's sort of, there's a little bit of me that's sort of won the lottery already.
So I just want to do more of that.
And I just want to keep learning in the sense that I think, you know, I'm 56 years old.
There's a bit of me that feels, well, I look at the buffets and the mongrels and the expertise that they had that I'm really early just beginning.
So, yeah, I think there's a lot to learn still.
